title: Present in every land
hookLine: the Jaap salutes the One who dwells in every country and every garb

lines: A MAP OF GURDWARAS, ZOOMED OUT.
THE PRAYERS WORK IN A NEW TIME ZONE.
cards: Open a map of gurdwaras on your phone and zoom out. Southall, in west London. Surrey, near Vancouver.
Yuba City in California. Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur, Melbourne, Singapore, a small town in northern Italy.
Behind each little marker, someone who left Punjab, carried the Guru's words in a suitcase, and found that the morning prayers still worked in a new time zone.
Long before any of that, the Tenth Guru wrote praise that fits every one of those places.

teach.b: Throughout Jaap, the One is saluted as dwelling everywhere: in every country, in every kind of dress, in water and on land.

teach.h: JALE HAIN, THALE HAIN: WATER AND LAND.
teach.b: One short chachari line says it in four words: jale hain, thale hain. You are in the water. You are on the land.
And near its very end, Jaap calls the One chatar chakkar vartee, present in all four directions, every point of the compass. Think about what every garb meant in the Guru's world.
Clothing told everyone who you were: a Hindu holy man's saffron, a Muslim scholar's robe, a soldier's armor, a farmer's rough cotton, a queen's silk.
Jaap salutes the One in all of them, and Sikhs read it plainly: no land is holier by birth, and no costume is closer to the Divine. Sikhs have long lived that line.
Tradition remembers Guru Nanak walking for years, east toward Assam, south toward Sri Lanka, north into the mountains, west as far as Mecca and Baghdad, sitting with people of every faith he met.

teach.h: SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: And today Sikhs pray the Ardas in Toronto and Birmingham and Bangkok with the same closing words you met at the end of year one: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of Punjab. The good of all.
In that reading, every land is somewhere to pray, and every stranger in every garb is someone the One is already with.

how: Sikhs around the world recite Jaap Sahib in the same words every morning, and gurdwaras far from Punjab close their gatherings with the Ardas's prayer for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

o: a country or land, any place on earth
a holy land where God lives most
a style of dress worn for prayer

games.q: present in every land — tap the pairs.

s: Jaap says some lands are closer to the Divine by birth
it salutes the One in every country and every garb.
tradition says Guru Nanak traveled as far as Mecca and Baghdad
his long journeys took him in every direction.
the Ardas asks for the good of Punjab alone
sarbat da bhala: the good of all.

games.q: you're a Sikh who has moved from Punjab to a new country with your gutka in your suitcase. does Jaap's praise still fit?
o: no: the prayers belong to Punjab.
yes: Jaap salutes the One in every land and every garb.
only in a gurdwara built like the ones at home.
games.why: jale hain, thale hain: in water and on land, in every country. the morning prayers work in every time zone.

practice: Choose a faraway place, somewhere you've never been, somewhere in the news, or the place your family came from, and picture the people there waking up or going to sleep right now.
Breathe in and picture them; breathe out and wish them well, plainly: may they be safe, may they be fed. If you pray, you can hold them in the words sarbat da bhala.
